events.title: The Fed raises interest rates
events.description: Its short-term target rises to 2.25–2.50% while the economy grows and the job market strengthens.

events.title: The Fed responds to coronavirus disruption
events.description: It cuts its short-term target to 0–0.25% and announces support for borrowing and financial markets.

events.title: Microsoft reports stronger cloud demand
events.description: Services delivered over the internet bring in more revenue as remote work grows. Advertising and some other sales are weaker.

events.title: Apple splits each share into four
events.description: Owners receive four shares for each one they held. The split alone does not make their investment worth more.

events.title: ExxonMobil reports a large annual loss
events.description: The company reports losing $22.4 billion in 2020, including reductions in the recorded value of assets, amid difficult energy markets.

what_happened_next.text:
Apple grew to more than five times its starting value and Microsoft to almost five times; Exxon Mobil ended about 13% lower. The five years brought changing interest rates and business conditions. In March 2020, the coronavirus outbreak disrupted daily life and work. The Federal Reserve cut interest rates close to zero and took steps to support markets and lending.

Microsoft said demand for cloud services grew as more people worked and learned from home, while some advertising and software sales weakened. Apple reported $59.7 billion in revenue for the quarter ending June 2020, 11% above a year earlier, and announced a share split. ExxonMobil reported a $22.4 billion loss for 2020 during a difficult year for energy companies. These are company facts from the period, not proof that one event alone determined each return.

The game ends in February 2021. No one starting in 2016 knew when a pandemic would arrive or how these companies would adapt. The results also show why a share split changes the number of shares but does not multiply the total value of an investment by itself.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: In 2016, Apple talked about its devices, Microsoft about its cloud services—online tools for storing information and using software—and Exxon Mobil about weak oil prices. The starting news also included community, health, science, and entertainment stories.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Over the next five years, the economy and the three companies changed in different ways. The pandemic changed how people lived and worked. No single headline tells the whole story of what happened to these investments.
reflection.what_faded_away: Football season and award shows passed, and new stories took their place. Those headlines were part of the day, but they could not tell people what would happen to the companies over five years.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: In February 2016, no one knew when a new coronavirus would spread around the world or how much it would change daily life and businesses. Nobody knew the emergency steps the Fed would take or how each company would respond.

hot:2016-02:apple.text: In July 2020, Apple reported $59.7 billion in revenue for the quarter ending in June, 11% more than a year earlier. It also announced a four-for-one share split. A split gives owners more shares but does not multiply the value of their investment by itself.

hot:2016-02:microsoft.text: In July 2020, Microsoft said demand for its cloud tools grew as people worked and learned from home. Its cloud services for business customers brought in more than $50 billion over the year. Some advertising and software sales were weaker, so different parts of the company felt the pandemic in different ways.

hot:2016-02:exxonmobil.text: ExxonMobil reported a $22.4 billion loss for 2020 as the pandemic reduced demand for fuel and other energy products. The company also recorded large, mostly non-cash charges. Its business remained important, but low demand and prices created a difficult year for oil producers.
